Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger

Negative Appraisals.value: I was betrayed by someone I trusted
There is something about me that made the event happen
People are not what they seem

vignette:
Leilani was eight when she stood frozen in the hallway, watching her father’s hand close around her mother’s throat. She remembered the sound—a wet gasp, the slap of skin. For years after, she told herself she should have done something, that there was something about her that made it happen, that she was the reason her mother stayed. That belief settled into her bones: people are not what they seem, and the ones you trust most will betray you.

Now thirty-one and a dancer with a small contemporary company in Honolulu, Leilani finds those childhood convictions surfacing in ways she cannot control. When a colleague calls out the name “David” during rehearsal—her father’s name—she feels a jolt of cold shame, and in that instant the old appraisal returns: *I was betrayed by someone I trusted*. She has come to believe that hearing that name is a sign that the past is still inside her, watching, waiting. The more she hears it, the more convinced she becomes that she is fundamentally flawed, that people will eventually show their true, dangerous selves. And that distrust then sharpens her attention: she scans the studio for anyone who might be watching her too closely, and every time she catches a gaze her chest tightens with the certainty that she is being judged, exposed.

The worst moments arrive without warning. Leilani will be in the middle of a turn, her heart pounding from the physical exertion, and suddenly the pumping in her chest is no longer about the dance—it is the sound of her own heartbeat during the violence, and the memory slams into her: the shame on recall, the feeling that she is back in that hallway, small and helpless. Sometimes, when the memory comes, she feels completely numb, as if the girl in the scene is a stranger. But more often the memory triggers a cascade: it reminds her of her intrinsic fault, and that thought loops straight back to the triggers. She begins to hear David’s name in conversations that do not contain it; she feels eyes on her even when no one is looking; her heart races not from the dance but from fear.

The stage, which once gave her freedom, has become the worst place. Being watched by an audience feels too much like being seen by her father that night. She has started to avoid the dressing room banter because someone might mention a name that could set her off. Six months ago she gave up a lead role, telling the artistic director she was injured. That lie cost her the trust of the company and strained her marriage—her husband cannot understand why she seems afraid of her own body on stage. Alone, she replays the memory, and with it the shame, and the shame tells her she has always been the problem.

What brought Leilani to therapy was a matinee last month. During a slow section, her heart began to pound from nothing—not the choreography, just the silence. The memory of her mother’s face, the shame, the betrayal, all came at once. She froze, walked offstage, and sat in the dark for an hour, shaking. She is afraid that if she cannot stop the cycles, she will lose the only thing she has ever loved. But she is also afraid of what she might find if she looks at the memory closely: that the fault really is hers, that she was always someone not to be trusted.
